title: Wadis: Desert Rivers That Come and Go
summary: How dry desert valleys called wadis suddenly fill with dangerous floods after heavy rain, and how that water brings life to the desert.
poll: A dry wadi is a safe place to play or camp at any time of year.

versions.title: Wadis in the Desert
versions.text:
Look out at the desert. Do you see a long, dry dip in the land? It may be a wadi.

A wadi is a valley. It looks like a river bed. But most days, it has no water. The sand is dry. So are the rocks.

Then a big storm comes. Rain falls hard. The ground is hard, too. The rain can not soak in fast. So it runs down. It fills the wadi. This is a flood.

A wadi flood can come fast. The rain may fall far off in the hills. You may not see a drop. But the flood can still reach you. It can sweep cars away. So stay out of a wadi when it rains.

When the flood ends, the water soaks in. It goes deep down. Wells fill up. Plants grow. Trees get a drink.

Long ago, folks made farms near wadis. In Riyadh, Wadi Hanifa is now a green park. Wadis bring life to the desert.

A flood in a wadi can come very fast. The rain may fall far away in the hills. You may not see a drop where you are. But the flood can still rush at you. It can even sweep away cars. That is why you should stay out of a wadi when it rains.

After the flood, the water starts to soak into the ground. It goes deep down. Wells fill up again. Plants and trees grow.

Long ago, people built farms and towns near wadis. In Riyadh, Wadi Hanifa is now a green park. Wadis bring life to the desert.

versions.title: Wadis: Desert Rivers That Come and Go
versions.text:
Look out across the desert, and you may notice a long, dry valley winding through the land. It might be a wadi. The word wadi is Arabic for a valley, and Saudi Arabia has thousands of them.

A wadi looks like the channel of a river. But for most of the year, it holds no water at all. Its sand and stones stay dry under the hot sun, and only a few tough plants grow there.

Then a storm arrives, and heavy rain falls in a short time. The desert ground is hard and dry, so the rain cannot soak in quickly. Instead, the water races downhill and pours into the wadi. The wadi suddenly becomes a fast, muddy river. This is called a flash flood.

A flash flood can arrive with almost no warning. The rain may fall far away in the mountains while the sky above you is blue. The sudden wall of water can sweep away cars and people. So you should never cross a wadi when water is flowing.

After the flood, much of the water slowly sinks into the ground and becomes groundwater. This water fills wells and feeds plants and trees. Some wadis even have an oasis, a green place with water in the desert. People also build a dam across some wadis to hold back floodwater.

For thousands of years, people have farmed near wadis. Wadi Al-Rummah is one of the longest wadis in Arabia. In Riyadh, Wadi Hanifa is now a green park.

versions.title: Wadis: Desert Rivers That Come and Go
versions.text:
If you gaze across the desert, you may notice a long, dry valley winding through the landscape, and it might be a wadi. The word wadi is Arabic for a valley, and Saudi Arabia contains thousands of them, stretching across its arid plains and rugged mountains.

A wadi resembles the channel of a river, but for most of the year it holds no water whatsoever. Its sand and stones bake under the scorching sun, and only a few hardy plants, such as acacia trees, manage to survive there. Over thousands of years, erosion from occasional floods carved these valleys into the rock, slowly wearing the land away.

Then a storm arrives, and heavy rain falls within a short period. Because the desert ground is hard and compacted, the rain cannot soak in quickly, so the water races downhill and pours into the wadi, which suddenly transforms into a fast, muddy torrent. This dangerous event is known as a flash flood.

A flash flood can arrive with almost no warning, because the rain may fall far away in the mountains while the sky above you remains clear. The sudden rush of water is powerful enough to sweep away vehicles and people, so you should never cross a wadi when water is flowing or camp inside one during the rainy season.

After the flood passes, much of the water gradually sinks into the ground, where it helps recharge the groundwater stored beneath the desert. This hidden supply refills wells and nourishes plants, while the floods also leave behind sediment, a layer of fine mud and sand that makes the soil fertile. In many locations, engineers construct dams across wadis to capture floodwater for later use.

For thousands of years, people have farmed and established settlements along wadis. Wadi Al-Rummah is one of the longest wadis in the Arabian Peninsula, and in Riyadh, Wadi Hanifa has been restored as a popular green park.

versions.title: Wadis: Desert Rivers That Come and Go
versions.text:
If you gaze across the desert, you may notice a long, dry valley winding through the landscape, and it might be a wadi, since the word wadi is Arabic for a valley, and Saudi Arabia contains thousands of them, stretching across its arid plains and rugged mountain ranges.

A wadi resembles the channel of a river, but for most of the year it holds no water whatsoever; its sand and stones bake beneath the scorching sun, and only a few hardy plants, such as acacia trees, manage to survive there. Over thousands of years, erosion caused by occasional floods carved these valleys into the rock, gradually wearing the landscape away.

Then a storm arrives, and torrential rain falls within a short period. Because the desert ground is hard and compacted, the rain cannot soak in quickly, so the water races downhill and pours into the wadi, which suddenly transforms into a fast, muddy torrent. This hazardous event is known as a flash flood.

A flash flood can arrive with almost no warning, because the rain may fall far away in the mountains while the sky above you remains perfectly clear. The sudden surge of water is powerful enough to sweep away vehicles and people, so you should never cross a wadi when water is flowing or camp inside one during the rainy season.

After the flood subsides, much of the water gradually seeps into the ground, where it helps recharge the groundwater stored beneath the desert. This hidden reserve replenishes wells and nourishes vegetation, while the floods also deposit sediment, a layer of fine mud and sand that makes the soil fertile. In numerous locations, engineers construct dams across wadis to capture floodwater for later use.

After heavy rain, the desert floor also comes briefly to life, because seeds that have rested in the dry soil for years sprout almost overnight, covering the wadi with grasses and wildflowers that attract insects, birds, and grazing animals.

For thousands of years, communities have farmed and established settlements along wadis. Wadi Al-Rummah is one of the longest wadis in the Arabian Peninsula, and in Riyadh, Wadi Hanifa has been restored as a popular green park.

versions.title: Wadis: Desert Rivers That Come and Go
versions.text:
If you gaze across the desert, you may notice a long, dry valley winding through the landscape, and it might well be a wadi, since the word wadi is Arabic for a valley, and Saudi Arabia contains thousands of them, stretching across its arid plains and rugged mountain ranges.

A wadi resembles the channel of a river, but for most of the year it contains no water whatsoever; its sand and stones bake beneath the scorching sun, and only a few hardy plants, such as acacia trees, manage to survive there. Over thousands of years, erosion caused by occasional floods carved these valleys into the rock, gradually wearing the landscape away.

Then a storm arrives, and torrential rain falls within a remarkably short period. Because the desert ground is hard and compacted, the rain cannot penetrate it quickly, so the water races downhill and pours into the wadi, which abruptly transforms into a fast, muddy torrent. This hazardous event is known as a flash flood, and it represents one of the most significant natural hazards in the region.

A flash flood can arrive with almost no warning, because the rain may fall far away in the mountains while the sky above you remains perfectly clear; the sudden surge of water is powerful enough to sweep away vehicles and people, so you should never attempt to cross a wadi when water is flowing or camp inside one during the rainy season.

After the flood subsides, much of the water gradually seeps into the ground, where it helps recharge the groundwater stored beneath the desert. This hidden reserve replenishes wells and nourishes vegetation, while the floods also deposit sediment, a layer of fine mud and sand that makes the soil considerably more fertile. In numerous locations, engineers construct dams across wadis to capture floodwater for later agricultural use.

After substantial rainfall, the desert floor also comes briefly to life, because dormant seeds that have rested in the parched soil for years germinate almost overnight, carpeting the wadi with grasses and wildflowers that attract insects, migrating birds, and grazing animals.

For thousands of years, communities have cultivated crops and established settlements along wadis. Wadi Al-Rummah is one of the longest wadis in the Arabian Peninsula, and in Riyadh, Wadi Hanifa has been restored as a popular green park.

versions.title: Wadis: Desert Rivers That Come and Go
versions.text:
If you gaze across the desert, you may notice a long, dry valley meandering through the landscape, and it might well be a wadi, since the word wadi is Arabic for a valley, and Saudi Arabia contains thousands of them, extending across its arid plains and rugged mountain ranges.

A wadi resembles the channel of a river, but for most of the year it contains no water whatsoever; its sand and stones bake beneath the scorching sun, and only a few resilient plants, such as acacia trees, manage to survive there. Over thousands of years, erosion caused by occasional floods carved these valleys into the bedrock, gradually wearing the surrounding landscape away through countless cycles of flooding.

Then a storm arrives, and torrential rain falls within a remarkably short period. Because the desert ground is hard and compacted, the rain cannot penetrate it quickly, so the water races downhill and pours into the wadi, which abruptly transforms into a powerful, muddy torrent. This hazardous phenomenon is known as a flash flood, and it represents one of the most significant natural hazards in the region.

A flash flood can arrive with almost no warning, because the rain may fall far away in the mountains while the sky above you remains perfectly clear. The sudden surge of water is powerful enough to sweep away vehicles and people, so you should never attempt to cross a wadi when water is flowing or camp inside one during the rainy season.

After the flood subsides, much of the water gradually seeps into the ground, where it helps recharge the groundwater stored beneath the desert. This hidden reserve replenishes wells and nourishes vegetation, while the floods also deposit sediment, a layer of fine mud and sand that makes the soil considerably more fertile. In numerous locations, engineers construct dams across wadis to capture floodwater for subsequent agricultural use.

After substantial rainfall, the desert floor also experiences a brief but spectacular revival, because dormant seeds that have rested in the parched soil for years germinate almost overnight, carpeting the wadi with grasses and wildflowers that attract insects, migrating birds, and grazing livestock.

For thousands of years, communities have cultivated crops and established permanent settlements along wadis, and today Wadi Al-Rummah is one of the longest wadis in the Arabian Peninsula, and in Riyadh, Wadi Hanifa has been carefully restored as a popular green park.

LOW.prompt: Write two rules to keep people safe near a wadi. Explain why each rule is important.
checklist: I explained each rule with a fact from the article.
I used at least two key words, such as flood or wadi.
LOW.modelAnswer: One rule is to never cross a wadi, or dry valley, when water is flowing in it, because a sudden flood can sweep away cars and people. Another rule is to never camp inside a wadi during the rainy season, because rain falling in the desert mountains can cause a flood even when the sky above you is clear. The hard, dry ground cannot soak up the rain fast enough, so the water rushes into the valley instead.

MID.prompt: Explain how a wadi can be both dangerous and helpful. Use at least two details from the article for each side.
checklist: I explained how a wadi can be dangerous.
I explained how a wadi can be helpful.
I used details and key words from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: A wadi can be dangerous because it is a dry channel that can transform within minutes into a sudden, fast-moving flash flood powerful enough to sweep away cars and people, even if the storm that caused it was far away in the mountains. A wadi can also be helpful, though, because after a flood passes, much of the water sinks into the ground and becomes groundwater that fills wells and feeds plants, and some wadis even form an oasis in the middle of the desert. People also build a dam across a wadi to capture floodwater so it can be used later instead of rushing away and being wasted.

HIGH.prompt: Wadis are described as both hazardous and essential. Explain which side you think matters more to people in Saudi Arabia, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I used at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I mentioned the other side and responded to it.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think the benefits of wadis matter more to people in Saudi Arabia than their dangers, even though both sides are real. In such an arid land, a wadi's ability to recharge groundwater after a storm, filling wells and nourishing an oasis, provides a water supply that desert communities have relied on for thousands of years, which is why towns and farms have always grown up beside them. It is true that a wadi can turn into a violent torrent carrying sediment, rocks, and branches with almost no warning, and this danger genuinely costs lives when people ignore the rules and cross flowing water. However, that danger can be managed through warnings, dams, and the simple choice to stay out of a wadi when water is flowing, while losing the water and recharge that wadis provide would threaten entire communities permanently.
